blocks.title: Diffraction
blocks.text: Diffraction of waves is the bending of waves around the sharp edges or corners of obstacles, or the spreading of waves beyond a barrier. It occurs when a wave encounters a physical barrier or an opening (a slit) that is comparable in size to the wavelength of the wave. The longer the wavelength, the greater the spreading, and vice versa.

blocks.alt: Two diagrams with the same gap in a barrier. Left: closely spaced straight wavefronts (small wavelength) pass the gap and spread only a little: Small wavelength, Small diffraction. Right: widely spaced wavefronts (large wavelength) spread out in wide half circles: Large wavelength, Large diffraction.
blocks.caption: Diffraction through a slit (PDF page 157): small wavelength, small diffraction; large wavelength, large diffraction (original drawing after the textbook's picture in this box).

blocks.text: Diffraction can be observed in various types of waves, including water waves, sound waves, light waves and electromagnetic waves. Some examples: hearing sound waves around corners or through a doorway from where they were generated, as sound waves bend around the corners; and the diffraction of X-rays by crystals, as the spacing between the regular arrays of atoms is of the order of the X-ray wavelength. Diffraction is a fundamental aspect of wave behaviour with many practical applications.

A ripple tank (Fig. 7.11) is a very useful apparatus not only to generate water waves but also to demonstrate wave properties such as reflection, diffraction and refraction. It contains water, a vibrator (for example a motorised oscillating needle), obstacles (for example a small rectangular block or a semicircular barrier) and gaps of different widths; a lamp above throws the wave pattern onto a white screen below the glass-bottomed tray. The vibrator creates a series of concentric circles or parallel waves, and an obstacle is placed to create a gap of a specific width; the experiment can be repeated with different gap widths. It is observed that when the gap width is small compared with the wavelength, diffraction is significant and the waves bend around the obstacle, creating a semicircular pattern; as the gap width increases relative to the wavelength, diffraction decreases and the waves pass through the gap with less bending. This demonstrates the qualitative effect of gap width on diffraction, and how the relationship between gap width and wavelength affects wave behaviour.

blocks.alt: A ripple tank: a glass bottomed tray of water in a frame on four legs. A vibrator bar hangs by elastic bands from wooden bars on a stand and touches the water surface. A lamp on the stand shines down from above, and a white screen on the floor below shows the wave pattern. Labels: Lamp, Stand, Vibrator, Water surface, Elastic bands, Frame, Glass bottomed tray, Leg, Wave pattern on screen, White screen.

Right: a wide gap, and the waves beyond stay mostly straight, curving only at the edges: Large gap, Decreased diffraction.

blocks.title: Example 7.6
blocks.text: In a ripple tank a wave generator produces 500 pulses in 10 s. Find the frequency of the pulses. Solution: n = 500 pulses, t = 10 s, f = ?. T = t/n = 10 s/500 = 1/50 s; f = 1/T = 1/(1/50 s) = 50 s^-1, so f = 50 pulses per second.

Diffraction of white light by a fine diffraction grating spreads it into colours (For Your Information). The fine rulings, each 0.5 um wide, on a compact disc act as a diffraction grating: when a small source of white light illuminates a disc, the diffracted light forms coloured lanes that are a composite of the diffraction patterns from the rulings (Interesting Information).
